opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is pretty simple. If you want to build AGI, you have two options: you can try to solve every problem in the world directly, or you can build something that solves the problem of building AI itself. Software engineering is the most direct lever on that second path. Almost everything we do in AI research, writing training code, building infrastructure, running experiments, debugging, is ultimately code. So if you can build a model that is a genuinely great software engineer, you've built something that can start contributing to its own improvement. That's the recursive loop that gets you to AGI much faster than doing everything by hand.

There's also a very practical reason. Code is one of the few domains where you get a really clean feedback signal. You can run it, you can test it, it either works or it doesn't. That makes it a great environment for training models to reason over long horizons, plan, verify their own work, and recover from mistakes, which are exactly the capabilities you need for general intelligence anyway. So it's not a narrow detour. It's a domain that forces you to solve the hard, general problems.

And then on top of that, it's enormously valuable on its own. Even before you get anywhere near AGI, a model that can reliably do real engineering work is a huge product. That lets you fund the research, get real-world usage, and learn from actual developers along the way. So for us, it's the rare case where the best commercial path and the best research path are the same path.

The last piece is why we've cared so much about things like long context. A real software engineer doesn't look at one file. They hold an entire codebase, its history, the docs, the conventions, all in their head. If you want a model to do that, you need it to work with a massive amount of context efficiently, and that ended up shaping a lot of the core technical bets we made.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong software engineer model could contribute to its own improvement, but does not clearly say it could automate the work of the people developing AGI.

r002.rationale: It does not mention recursively improving alignment.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a recursive loop in which a strong software engineer model contributes to its own improvement.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss replicating AI researchers or overcoming a scarcity of human research expertise.

r005.rationale: It argues software engineering develops general capabilities, but does not characterize it as a minimum viable form of AGI that can build all other needed capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that software engineering is the one domain where, if you crack it, you get almost everything else for free.

Here's how I think about it. AGI isn't a single moment; it's a system that can do useful cognitive work across a very wide range of tasks, and that can get better at doing that work. If you have a model that can genuinely write, read, and reason about code at the level of a strong engineer, you have a model that can build tools, run experiments, analyze data, and ultimately help improve itself. Code is the universal interface to doing things in the world. Almost every other knowledge-work task eventually routes through it, whether that's running a scientific simulation, automating a business process, or building the next version of the model.

The second reason is that it's measurable. A lot of domains are fuzzy. With code, you have tests, you have compilers, you have real users with real bugs. That gives you a feedback signal that's much cleaner than "did this essay sound good." Clean feedback is what lets you actually climb.

The third thing, and this is where Magic is a bit different, is that real software engineering isn't about writing a function in isolation. It's about holding a huge amount of context in your head at once. A codebase with millions of lines, the documentation, the conversation history with your teammates, the thing that broke last Tuesday. Human engineers are limited by what they can keep in working memory. If you give a model the ability to attend over essentially the whole context, not a retrieval approximation of it but the real thing, you're removing a constraint that humans have never been able to remove. That's not just "a better coding assistant." That's a different kind of collaborator.

So when I say automating software engineering is a path to AGI, I mean it quite literally. Build a system that can act as a full engineer on a real codebase, at scale, with full context. Once you have that, the system can participate in building the next system. That loop is the whole game.

r001.rationale: It says a model with strong engineering ability can improve itself and participate in building the next system, conveying that it could do work involved in developing AGI.

r002.rationale: It does not propose using automated software engineering to improve alignment, recursively or otherwise.

r003.rationale: It says a capable coding model can help improve itself and build the next version of the model.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss replicating AI researchers or overcoming a scarcity of human research expertise.

r005.rationale: It calls software engineering the domain where cracking it yields almost everything else, and says code can build tools and support other knowledge-work tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think software engineering is a useful path because it forces you to solve a lot of the problems that matter for general intelligence. Writing a small function is one thing. Taking an ambiguous goal, understanding a large codebase, making a plan, and figuring out why your approach failed—that requires a much broader set of capabilities.

And software gives you a way to test whether you’re making progress. You can run the code, get feedback, and iterate. That doesn’t tell you whether you’ve satisfied every aspect of the user’s intent, but it gives you a powerful learning signal.

The other piece is that AI research itself involves a lot of software engineering. If you can automate more of that work, you can accelerate the process of building better AI. So I wouldn’t say that a system that writes code is automatically AGI. The idea is that solving software engineering deeply pushes you toward general capabilities, while also giving you tools to accelerate the research.

r001.rationale: It says automating software engineering could accelerate AI research, but does not say a capable software engineer could automate the work of people developing AGI.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose recursively improving alignment.

r003.rationale: It says automation could accelerate building better AI, but does not propose recursively improving AI models.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss replicating computerized AI researchers or overcoming a scarcity of human research expertise.

r005.rationale: It describes software engineering as a path toward general capabilities, but does not call it a minimum viable form of AGI or say it could build all other needed capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Because software engineering is a very broad intelligence task. You have to understand what someone wants, reason about a complex system, make a plan, write code, test it, and revise your approach when something doesn’t work. If you can automate that whole process reliably, you’re developing capabilities that extend well beyond coding.

Software also gives you a useful feedback loop: you can run what you’ve built and see whether it works. That makes it a powerful environment for training systems to solve increasingly difficult problems.

And then there’s the research side. AI research involves a lot of software engineering. As these systems become more capable, they can help us build better AI systems. That’s why we see it as both a valuable application in its own right and a path toward more general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems can help build better AI systems, but does not explain that a sufficiently capable software engineer could automate the work of people developing AGI.

r003.rationale: It says increasingly capable systems can help build better AI systems, describing software-engineering capability as a way to improve AI systems.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss replicating AI researchers or overcoming a shortage of human research expertise.

r005.rationale: It calls software engineering a broad intelligence task and a path toward general intelligence, but does not characterize it as a minimum viable form of AGI that could build other needed capabilities.
